summary: A 1970 note with thoughts and reflections on RFC 54, which it updates. It is a discussion contribution from two authors.

eli5.summary: The authors share their thinking about an earlier note, like a response to a classmate's essay.

subtitle: Harvard proposes typed error codes, a separate overflow command and a reset handshake for crashed hosts.

tldr.problem: RFC 54 reported both real errors and resource overflow in ways that misled users, and gave no way to recover when a host crashed and restarted.
tldr.mechanism: The authors propose an 8-bit error type in the ERR message, a new OVF command for overflow, and RST and RSR commands to reset and re-announce a host.
tldr.outcome: These ideas were left out of the official protocol and are offered for discussion and possible inclusion in the second level protocol.

today: RFC 57 updates RFC 54 as a discussion paper and has not been obsoleted. Its status is Unknown, and the commands it proposes were suggestions for a later protocol level.

sections.title: Ideas Left Out of RFC 54
sections.content:
Mike Kraley and John Newkirk of Harvard wrote this on June 19, 1970. While writing RFC 54 several new ideas appeared that had not been discussed or were too imprecise, so they were not put in the official protocol. They are offered here as subjects for discussion and for later inclusion in the second level protocol.

There are two groups of ideas: errors and overflow, and what to do when a host goes down and comes back.
sections.eli5: While writing the official rules, the authors had extra ideas that were not ready, so they put them in a separate note to talk about.

sections.title: Errors Versus Overflow
sections.content:
Following the discussion in RFC 48, the authors want two kinds of error kept apart. A real error, such as a request for connection made of two send sockets, can only come from a broken NCP. An overflow happens when finite resources run out, for example when there is no room to create tables and queues for an incoming request. Nobody did anything incorrect, and recovery just means repeating the request later.

RFC 54 reported overflow by returning a CLS, as if the connection were refused. The initiating user is then misinformed, which matters in some algorithms. They propose a new control command, OVF, carrying my socket and your socket (32-bit socket numbers matching the rejected request). An incoming OVF acts like an incoming CLS, and the user is also told that the foreign host's resources were overtaxed, not that he was refused. They considered adding an 8-bit field to CLS instead but judged that conceptually inferior and harder to implement.

They also propose extending the ERR message with an 8-bit field after the op code naming the type of error, followed by the length and text fields as before.
sections.eli5: 'You did it wrong' and 'I am too full right now' are different messages, so they should have different names.

sections.title: Host Up and Host Down
sections.content:
A soft crash comes with prior notice, so there is time for pre-recovery steps. A hard crash gives little warning, and the machine's state after recovery is rarely predictable. After a hard crash the NCP's data structures are probably destroyed, and the network has declared the host dead only to processes that tried to send data and were refused.

The authors propose two control commands, RESET (RST) and RESET REPLY (RSR), each just an op code with no parameters. On receiving an RST, a host immediately terminates all connections with the sender without sending any CLS, notes that the sender is alive, and echoes an RSR. On receiving an RSR, a host notes that the echoing host is alive. A host live table, as described in RFC 55, can then be assembled and connections can resume.

They note an open problem: the network may still carry messages sent before the crash, and the facilities for unblocking links or discarding messages do not exist yet, so more work with BBN is needed. Soft crashes need more complex solutions, and the authors say a good initialization and recovery protocol is far more necessary.
sections.eli5: When a computer wakes up after a crash, it shouts 'reset!', everyone forgets their old chats with it, and each answers 'I am here', so the chats can start fresh.

sections.title: Nine Proposed Error Types
sections.content:
While writing the pseudo-Algol program mentioned in RFC 55, the authors distinguished nine error types, plus an unspecified one numbered 0. The list appears in the table after the Errors Versus Overflow section.

The note ends by thanking Steve Crocker and Jon Postel for conversations, and Jim Balter and Charles Kline of UCLA for help with the pseudo-Algol program.
sections.eli5: They made a numbered list of the kinds of mistakes a program can notice, so a message can say exactly which one happened.
